newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Thai PM arrives for talks with feuding Cambodians.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM arrives for talks with feuding Cambodians.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh flew in to Phnom Penh on Saturday for a one-day visit that diplomats said he would use to express concern over Cambodia's simmering political crisis.

Chavalit was welcomed at Phnom Penh airport by Foreign Minister Ung Huot and headed into the city where he was due to meet First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and his uneasy coalition partner, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.

Diplomats in Phnom Penh said Chavalit was bound to discuss fears about political stability in Cambodia with the feuding premiers and urge them to resolve their differences as the country prepared to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"I'm sure he will," said one senior diplomat from the region. "Everbody is expressing their concern. But I think it will be coupled with encouragement for the two to work together and overcome their present difficulties, especially now as they are joining ASEAN."
Cambodia, Burma and Laos are due to become full ASEAN members next month. ASEAN comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Chavalit's visit coincides with growing international concern over rising political violence in Cambodia.
Bodyguards loyal to the two premiers fought a brief but fierce street battle in Phnom Penh on Tuesday night which left two people dead.
Officials have played down the incident, saying it was an isolated dispute between groups of security men, but analysts said it illustrated the potential for explosive confrontation.

A long-running power-struggle between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, which is at the heart of their feud, has intensified in recent weeks with the apparent self-destruction of the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and bitter disagreement over how to handle the remnants of the rebel army.

Ranariddh is trying to strike a deal with a faction he has said broke away from hated Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot earlier this month, while Hun Sen is trying to prevent any move that would strengthen his rival's hand prior to elections next year.
The breakaway Khmer Rouge faction reported on Friday that it had captured Pol Pot but officials in Phnom Penh said they were sceptical of the claim.

Thailand was a key supporter of the Khmer Rouge, royalist forces and another non-communist guerrilla group during the 1980s when the rebel alliance battled a Vietnamese army of occupation and the Hanoi-backed government in Phnom Penh.

All outside powers agreed to cease support for the Cambodian factions after a 1991 peace treaty but subsequent Cambodian allegations of continued Thai support for the Khmer Rouge soured relations between Bangkok and Phnom Penh for several years.

An official at the Thai embassy in Phnom Penh played down speculation that the issue of Pol Pot would be raised in talks between Chavalit and his Cambodian counterparts. The Khmer Rouge was an internal Cambodian affair, he said.
The Thai official said agreements on the opening of seven crossing points along the two countries' common border and on cultural cooperation would be signed on Saturday.
Chavalit was due to meet Queen Monineath Sihanouk later on Saturday. King Norodom Sihanouk is in Beijing for medical treatment.
